Elizabeth had grown sorrowful and dispirited. Her customary pursuits no longer pleased her; enjoyment of any kind seemed an offense against the dead. She believed endless grief and weeping the fitting homage to innocence so cruelly ruined. Gone was the happy girl who once wandered beside the lake with me and spoke rapturously of our future. The first of those afflictions sent to loosen our hold upon the world had reached her, and its darkening influence put out her loveliest smiles.

“When I consider, dear cousin,” she said, “the wretched death of Justine Moritz, the world and all its doings look quite different to me. Formerly, the wickedness and injustice I encountered in books or others’ accounts seemed stories of bygone times or imagined evils. At least they were distant, things understood by reason rather than felt by imagination. Now suffering has entered our own home, and people seem monsters thirsting for one another’s blood. Yet surely I judge them unfairly. Everyone thought that poor girl guilty. Had she committed the crime for which she died, she would indeed have been among the most depraved creatures alive. To kill her benefactor and friend’s son for a few jewels—a child she had tended since birth and apparently loved as her own! I could never approve the death of any person, but I should certainly have judged such a being unworthy of human society. Yet she was innocent. I know it, I feel it; and your agreement strengthens my conviction. Alas, Victor, if falsehood can resemble truth so closely, who can count upon secure happiness? I feel myself upon the brink of a cliff, with thousands pressing towards me to cast me into the gulf. William and Justine have been murdered, and their murderer escapes. He wanders freely through the world, perhaps held in esteem. But even were I sentenced to the scaffold for those same crimes, I would never exchange my place for his.”

Her words caused me the most dreadful anguish. Though not by my own hand, I was in effect the real murderer. Elizabeth saw my torment in my face. Taking my hand affectionately, she said, “My dearest friend, you must grow calm. God knows how profoundly these events have wounded me, but I am not so miserable as you.

He was intensely sullen, and “that damned bug” was all he said throughout the journey. I carried two shuttered lanterns. Legrand took only the beetle, tied to a length of whipcord, which he swung back and forth like a magician as he walked. This final, unmistakable sign of my friend’s disturbed mind nearly brought me to tears. I decided, however, that I should indulge his fancy for the moment, at least until I could take stronger action with some prospect of success. Meanwhile, I tried unsuccessfully to discover the expedition’s purpose. Having persuaded me to join him, he apparently had no wish to discuss anything of lesser importance. Every question received the same answer: “We shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s northern end in a small boat. Climbing the high ground on the mainland shore, we headed northwest through an extremely wild, deserted landscape without a single visible human footprint. Legrand led confidently, stopping only briefly now and then to consult what looked like landmarks he had established on an earlier visit.

We traveled like this for about two hours. As the sun was setting, we entered country far bleaker than anything we had yet crossed. It was a sort of plateau near the top of a nearly inaccessible hill, densely wooded from bottom to summit. Huge rocks stood scattered among the trees, apparently resting loose on the soil. Many seemed kept from crashing into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines ran in several directions, adding to the landscape’s grim solemnity.

The natural platform we had climbed onto was so thickly covered with brambles that we soon realized we could never get through without the scythe. At his master’s direction, Jupiter began cutting a path to the base of an extraordinarily tall tulip tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, towering above them all. Its beautiful shape and leaves, its widely spreading branches, and its overall majesty surpassed not only those oaks but every other tree I had ever seen.

“At the center of the opening I saw a white spot, though I could not initially identify it. I adjusted the telescope’s focus and looked again. This time I recognized a human skull.

“That discovery made me confident enough to regard the puzzle as solved. The words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could refer only to the skull’s position in the tree. And in the context of buried treasure, ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ had only one possible meaning. I understood that a bullet should be dropped through the skull’s left eye. A straight line drawn from the nearest point of the trunk through the ‘shot’—the place where the bullet landed—and extended another fifty feet would mark a precise location. I thought it at least possible that something valuable lay buried beneath that point.”

“That is all extremely clear,” I said. “Clever, but simple and explicit. What happened after you left the Bishop’s Hotel?”

“After carefully noting the tree’s direction, I headed home. The moment I moved from the ‘devil’s seat,’ however, the circular opening disappeared. Turn as I might, I could not see it again. To me, the most ingenious part of the arrangement is that the opening can be seen from no accessible position except that narrow ledge on the rock face. Repeated attempts have convinced me this is a fact.

“Jupiter accompanied me on that visit to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel.’ He had doubtless noticed my distracted behavior over the previous weeks and was especially careful never to leave me alone. But next morning I rose very early, managed to slip away, and went into the hills to find the tree. After considerable effort I located it. When I returned that night, my servant proposed to give me a beating. I believe you know the remainder of the adventure as well as I do.”

“I suppose,” I said, “our first attempt at digging missed the right place because Jupiter foolishly dropped the beetle through the skull’s right eye instead of its left.”

“Exactly. That mistake shifted the ‘shot’—the peg nearest the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been buried directly beneath it, the error would hardly have mattered. But the ‘shot’ and the nearest point on the trunk were merely two points defining a direction. Naturally, the error, small as it was at the beginning, grew as we extended the line. By the time we reached fifty feet, we were completely off course.
